title: Composition, context, forms, performance
blurb: Context, compound components, forms, optimistic updates, accessibility and routing — the parts of React you get asked about once past the basics.

questions.q: What does Context cost you, compared with passing props?
choices: Nothing: it replaces a state library with no downsides at any scale
Its values are global, so they persist across full page reloads
Every consumer re-renders whenever the provided value changes
It memoises the subtree below, so children can show stale values
questions.why: Context is dependency injection, not a state manager. If a fast-changing value shares a provider with a slow-changing one, every consumer re-renders; split the contexts or memoise the value. It holds nothing across reloads.
questions.asked: 'When would you use context?' The weak answer is 'instead of Redux, for all state'.

questions.q: Why does this provider re-render every consumer on each parent render?
choices: The object literal is a new reference on every render
Providers always re-render every consumer, whatever the value
`setTheme` from `useState` changes identity every render
Context compares values deeply, which forces the re-render
questions.why: Context compares the value with `Object.is`, and `{{ ... }}` is a new object each time. Wrap it: `useMemo(() => ({ theme, setTheme }), [theme])`. `setTheme` is already stable, so it is not the cause.
questions.asked: It tests whether you can spot the reference-equality cost of context in code review.

questions.q: What is prop drilling?
choices: Passing so many props to one component that its signature is unreadable
Mutating a prop inside a child so the parent sees the changed value
Forwarding every prop to a child with the spread syntax `{...props}`
Passing props through components that do not use them, to reach a child
questions.why: It is usually fine at two or three levels: explicit and greppable. Reaching for context at the first sign of it replaces a visible data flow with an invisible one, and composition (passing elements as children) often removes the drilling with no context at all.
questions.asked: The follow-up, 'is it always bad?', is where the composition answer earns credit.

questions.q: `count` lives in the parent. Why can `Slow` re-render without re-rendering `Fast`?
choices: React memoises `children` automatically for every component
`children` was created by the parent, so the element is unchanged
It cannot: `children` always re-renders along with its parent
Only because `Slow` is a class component with its own lifecycle
questions.why: The `<Fast>` element object was made in the parent's render. If `Slow` re-renders for its own reasons, React sees the identical element and skips that subtree. It is memoisation without `memo`, and React does not memoise `children` in general.
questions.asked: A sophisticated answer to 'how would you optimise this tree?'.

questions.q: What are compound components?
choices: Components that render other components inside their own JSX
Components that share implicit state through context, like Tabs and Tab
Functions that take a component and return an enhanced component
Components whose logic is assembled from several different custom hooks
questions.why: `<Tabs><Tab /></Tabs>` lets the consumer compose markup naturally instead of passing a config array. The cost is a less explicit API and a required parent, so the pattern earns its place mainly in design systems. A function that returns an enhanced component is a higher-order component, a different pattern.
questions.asked: It comes up when designing reusable UI, and shows familiarity with how component libraries are built.

questions.q: What is an optimistic update?
choices: Retrying a failed request automatically until the server accepts it
Prefetching data the user is likely to need before they ask for it
Skipping error handling on the assumption the server stays healthy
Showing the change in the UI at once and rolling back if it fails
questions.why: It makes an app feel instant. It needs the previous state kept for rollback and a visible message when the rollback happens; silently reverting is worse than a spinner.
questions.asked: Common for frontend roles; the follow-up is 'how do you handle the failure case?'.

questions.q: Which validation timing avoids flagging a field while the user is still typing, yet clears the error as soon as it is fixed?
choices: Validate on blur, then on change once the field has shown an error
Validate on every keystroke from the moment the field is focused
Validate only on submit, and keep errors until the next submit
Validate only on the server and show its errors after a round trip
questions.why: Keystroke validation shows 'invalid email' after the second character. Validating on blur waits until the user leaves the field; switching that field to live validation once it has errored lets the message clear as they fix it. The server must validate regardless.
questions.asked: It tests form UX judgement, which separates developers who have watched users fill in forms.

questions.q: Your React form's Submit can be clicked twice before the first request returns. What is the client-side fix?
choices: Debounce the submit handler by 300 ms so rapid clicks collapse
Wrap the submit handler in `useCallback` so it is created once
Track an in-flight flag in state and disable the button while set
Call `event.preventDefault()` at the top of the submit handler
questions.why: A `submitting` flag set before the request and cleared after it blocks the second click for exactly as long as needed. A debounce only delays, `useCallback` changes identity not behaviour, and `preventDefault` stops navigation, not a second call. The server still needs idempotency for retries; that is a separate, server-side fix.
questions.asked: Double submits create duplicate orders; interviewers want the client fix and awareness of the server half.

questions.q: What makes a modal dialog accessible?
choices: A high z-index and a dark overlay, so it is visually on top
Rendering it in a portal, so it sits at the end of the body
Setting `aria-hidden` on the modal until it has fully opened
Focus moves in and stays inside, Escape closes it, and it is labelled
questions.why: It also needs `role="dialog"`, an inert background, and focus returned to the opener on close. A portal fixes stacking and overflow, not accessibility: tab order follows the DOM, so you still have to trap focus inside the dialog yourself.
questions.asked: A strong mid-level signal: most candidates only mention the overlay.

questions.q: What is a portal for?
choices: Loading a component's code lazily the first time it is shown
Rendering a component on the server and streaming it to the client
Rendering into a DOM node elsewhere, while keeping React context
Sharing state between two routes without lifting it to the root
questions.why: It escapes `overflow: hidden` and z-index stacking for modals, tooltips and toasts. Context still flows and synthetic events still bubble through the React tree, which surprises people expecting DOM behaviour.
questions.asked: It usually leads into 'so where do events from a portal bubble?'.

questions.q: Why put a table's filters in the URL query string?
choices: Reading the URL is faster than reading component state
The view can be shared, bookmarked, refreshed and navigated back to
It reduces re-renders, because the router batches the updates
The server requires filters in the URL so it can cache the responses
questions.why: 'Send me that filtered view' is a real user need, and back/forward come free. The rule of thumb: state that describes what you are looking at belongs in the URL. It is not a performance technique.
questions.asked: A design question that shows product sense as well as React knowledge.

questions.q: What does list virtualisation do?
choices: Mounts only the rows in view plus a buffer, whatever the list length
Loads the next page of data from the API as the user scrolls down
Caches every rendered row in memory so scrolling back is instant
Compresses the list data so that it takes less memory in the browser
questions.why: 10,000 rows means 10,000 DOM nodes and a frozen page; virtualising keeps about 30 mounted. Loading more data is infinite scroll, a separate concern. The costs: variable row heights are hard, and Ctrl-F stops finding off-screen rows.
questions.asked: The standard answer to 'this table with 10,000 rows is slow'.

questions.q: From an engineering view, how does infinite scroll differ from numbered pagination?
choices: They are the same data fetching, only styled differently in the UI
Infinite scroll is always faster, because it never refetches data
It needs cursor paging and accumulated state; pages can use offsets
Pagination must be server-side, while infinite scroll is client-only
questions.why: Offset paging over a live dataset duplicates or skips rows as items are inserted, which shows up badly when pages are appended. Infinite scroll also hides the footer, loses the scroll position on back navigation, and needs a keyboard-accessible alternative.
questions.asked: A product-engineering question: the strong answer names the data problem and the UX costs.

questions.q: How do you make a component work both controlled and uncontrolled?
choices: Use internal state only when the optional `value` prop is undefined
Keep internal state always, and sync the `value` prop in with an effect
Export two separate components, one controlled and one uncontrolled
Keep the value in a ref in both cases and read it on each change
questions.why: This 'controllable' pattern is used by every component library: `const isControlled = value !== undefined`. Syncing a prop into state with an effect gives two sources of truth and a render of lag.
questions.asked: It separates people who have built reusable components from people who have only consumed them.

questions.q: What is the keyboard contract for a dropdown menu?
choices: Tab moves between the items, and Enter selects the currently focused item
Only mouse interaction is needed, as long as there is a label
Space opens each submenu, and Tab moves between the submenus
Arrows move between items, Enter selects, Escape closes, Tab leaves
questions.why: Roving tabindex: the menu is one tab stop and arrows move within it. Making every item tabbable is the common mistake: it forces a keyboard user through 40 stops to get past your menu.
questions.asked: It checks whether you have built an accessible widget rather than only a styled one.

questions.q: What should a good component test assert on?
choices: A snapshot of every component's full rendered output
What the user sees and does: text, roles and interactions
The values of each hook's internal state after each action
Nothing at unit level: only end-to-end tests are reliable
questions.why: Tests coupled to implementation break on every refactor and let real bugs through. Querying by role also catches accessibility problems for free. Snapshots of everything turn into approval noise nobody reads.
questions.asked: The Testing Library philosophy question; expect it for any React role that mentions tests.

questions.q: What is wrong with this line?
choices: `useState` cannot take a prop as its initial value
It reads the prop only once, so later changes are ignored
It causes an infinite loop when `props.value` changes
It copies the prop by reference, so edits mutate the parent
questions.why: `useState`'s argument is only the initial value. If you meant 'reset when the prop changes', change the key; if you meant a default, name the prop `defaultValue` so the one-shot behaviour is documented.
questions.asked: A common review comment; the strong answer offers both fixes and says when each applies.

questions.q: You are asked to make a slow page faster. What do you do first?
choices: Wrap the heavier components in `React.memo`
Add `useMemo` around the costly-looking calculations
Split the bundle so less JavaScript loads at startup
Profile it to see what re-renders and for how long
questions.why: The React Profiler tells you which component, how often and how long. Optimising by guesswork usually adds complexity, moves nothing, and sometimes makes it slower.
questions.asked: Whether you measure before optimising is one of the clearest seniority signals there is.

questions.q: What is code splitting in a React app?
choices: Loading route or feature bundles on demand with `lazy` and Suspense
Splitting large components into several smaller source files
Separating the CSS from the JavaScript into different bundles
Running independent components in parallel on separate threads
questions.why: The usual first cut is per route. Watch for a waterfall: lazy-loading a component that then fetches its own data serialises two round trips. File structure alone changes nothing about what the browser downloads.
questions.asked: The first answer to 'our bundle is 3 MB', and the waterfall follow-up shows depth.

questions.q: What does a router give you beyond swapping components on screen?
choices: Faster rendering, because routes are compiled ahead of time
Server-side rendering of every route with no extra configuration
URL state, back and forward, deep links, and per-route loading
Automatic authentication checks on every route it matches
questions.why: The URL becomes state the browser understands, so history and links work. Per route, it can also start data loading before the component renders and split the code so each route downloads only what it needs. Authentication is still something you wire in.
questions.asked: It checks you can justify the dependency, not just that you have used one.

questions.q: When is a global client-state store justified over context plus local state?
choices: As soon as two components anywhere in the app share one value
For any app with more than about ten components in its tree
Never: context plus local state always scales far enough
When many unrelated components read and write shared state often
questions.why: Much of what used to go in Redux is server cache, which a data-fetching library handles better. What remains (session, UI shell, cross-cutting toggles) is often small enough for context, until frequent updates from many places make re-render scope matter.
questions.asked: Distinguishing server state from client state is the strong move.

questions.q: What is the risk of `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`?
choices: It is slow, because React re-parses the HTML on every render
It breaks the virtual DOM diff for every sibling of the element
It inserts raw HTML, so unsanitised content becomes an XSS hole
It only works in development builds and is stripped in production
questions.why: React escapes interpolated values by default, which is why XSS is rare in React apps; this prop is the explicit opt-out. Sanitise with a library such as DOMPurify, and never pass raw user input.
questions.asked: A quick security filter for any frontend role that renders user content.

questions.q: What undo/redo approach does immutable state make almost free?
choices: Re-fetching the previous version of the data from the server
Keeping past, present and future stacks of state snapshots
Storing the last value in a ref and restoring it on undo
Recording DOM mutations and replaying them in reverse
questions.why: With immutable updates each state is a snapshot you can keep without copying, so undo is moving entries between stacks. Diff-based designs (command pattern, Immer patches) also work but need more code. It is the strongest practical argument for not mutating state.
questions.asked: It links immutability to a feature users want, which is how interviewers test if the principle stuck.

questions.q:
In `

Title

`, what does `Card` receive as `children`?
choices: The `<h2>` element, to place wherever it likes
The string `'Title'`, with the tag stripped off
Nothing: `Card` must read its own DOM children
An array holding a single rendered DOM node
questions.why: Anything between a component's tags arrives as `props.children`, here a React element, not a DOM node. `Card` decides where to render it, which is how layout components wrap content they know nothing about.
questions.asked: The basis of composition; everything from layouts to compound components builds on it.

questions.q: What is a render prop?
choices: A boolean prop that decides whether a component renders at all
A prop that holds pre-rendered HTML as a string to be inserted
A function prop the component calls to render, passing it data
A prop that forces a child to re-render when its value changes
questions.why: `<List items={users} renderItem={(u) => <UserRow user={u} />} />` lets the component own the looping or the logic while the caller owns the markup. Hooks replaced many render props for sharing logic, but they remain common for customising what a component draws.
questions.asked: It checks you can read older library APIs and know when the pattern still fits.

questions.q: Why did hooks replace most higher-order components (HOCs)?
choices: Hooks share logic without wrappers, avoiding hidden or clashing props
HOCs stopped working with function components after React 16.8
Hooks run faster, because HOCs force an extra render on every update
HOCs cannot pass props down, so each one needed its own context
questions.why: Stacking `withRouter(withAuth(withTheme(Page)))` produced wrapper hell, props injected from nowhere, and name collisions between HOCs. A hook call makes the dependency explicit in the component body. HOCs still work; they are just rarely the best tool now.
questions.asked: Older codebases are full of HOCs; this checks you can maintain them and explain the move away.

questions.q: What is the container/presentational split?
choices: Putting every component inside a CSS container for layout
Class components hold the state; function components hold the UI
Wrapping pages in a container that catches errors from children
One component loads and manages data; another only renders props
questions.why: The presentational component is easy to test and reuse because it only turns props into markup; the container deals with fetching and state. Hooks made the split less rigid, but keeping data access out of reusable UI is still good practice.
questions.asked: It shows whether you think about where data access belongs in a component tree.

questions.q: What is this pattern called, and what does it give `Layout`?
choices: Render props: `Layout` calls each prop to get its markup
Slot props: named places for content `Layout` knows nothing of
Compound components: they share state with `Layout` implicitly
Higher-order components: each prop wraps `Layout` in a new layer
questions.why: Elements passed as named props work like extra `children`: `Layout` only decides where they go. The parent keeps ownership of their props and state, so no drilling is needed. They are elements, not functions, which is what distinguishes them from render props.
questions.asked: Slots are the composition answer to prop drilling, and interviewers like candidates who reach for them.

questions.q: This edit form mounts while `user` is still loading, then stays empty. Which fix also keeps the user's edits when the data refetches in the background?
choices: Copy `user` into state in an effect that depends on `user`
Render the form only once `data` exists, keyed by `data.id`
Copy `user.name` into state during render whenever the `user` object changes
Pass `user.name` as the input's `value` with no local state
questions.why: Mounting after load gives `useState` the real initial value, and keying by id resets the form only for a different user. A refetch returns a new object with the same id, so edits survive; the effect and the render-time copy both fire on the new object reference and overwrite them. Without local state the input cannot be edited.
questions.asked: Every CRUD app has an edit screen; this is the bug they all hit first.

questions.q: Users delete emails often and occasionally by mistake. Which delete UX serves them best?
choices: A confirm dialog on every delete, so mistakes are always caught
Disable delete for items the user has opened in the last hour
Require the user to type the item's name before each delete
Delete at once and offer Undo in a toast for a few seconds
questions.why: Frequent confirm dialogs get clicked through by habit, so they add friction without catching mistakes. Undo keeps the common case fast and makes the rare mistake cheap. Typed confirmation suits rare, irreversible actions such as deleting a whole project.
questions.asked: A product-sense question; strong candidates match the safeguard to how often and how reversible the action is.

questions.q: When is a skeleton screen better than a spinner?
choices: When the layout of the incoming content is known in advance
When the request usually takes under 100 ms to return
When the request might fail and needs a retry button
When the page is rendered on the server, never the client
questions.why: A skeleton reserves the shape of the content, so the page does not jump when data arrives and the wait feels shorter. For very fast responses, showing nothing for a moment avoids a flash of either.
questions.asked: It shows attention to perceived performance and layout shift, which users notice.

questions.q: Why do larger React codebases group files by feature rather than by type, such as `components/` and `hooks/`?
choices: Bundlers can only code-split folders that contain a whole feature
React requires a component's custom hooks to live in the same folder as the component
Code that changes together lives together, so a feature is easy to find and delete
Grouping by type causes circular imports that break hot module reloading
questions.why: A change to 'invoices' then touches one folder instead of five, and removing a feature is deleting a directory. Bundlers split on dynamic imports, not folders, and React has no rule about file layout.
questions.asked: It checks whether you have worked in a codebase big enough for structure to matter.

questions.q: What is the main cost of a polymorphic `as` prop, as in `<Button as="a" href="/x">`?
choices: It forces a remount whenever the `as` value changes between renders
React cannot render a tag name that arrives as a string prop
It removes the element from the accessibility tree entirely
Typing it well is hard, since the allowed props must follow `as`
questions.why: `href` is valid only when `as="a"`, so correct types need generics over the element type; naive versions accept invalid combinations or lose autocomplete. React renders string tag names fine. The pattern is worth it in design systems, less so in app code.
questions.asked: It probes design-system experience and TypeScript depth at the same time.
